title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial (N=150 synthetic intents; paired baseline vs guarded; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to test whether constrained prompting plus deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair) increases semantic correctness when translating operator natural-language intents into low-level network configuration sequences. Model: gpt-5-mini; verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Primary outcome: verifier pass/fail per intent. Results: baseline = 149/150 (99.33%), guarded = 150/150 (100.0%), paired absolute difference = 0.67 percentage points, exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150). Interpretation: on this synthetic corpus the guarded workflow produced no statistically or practically meaningful improvement over a near-ceiling baseline; the outcome illustrates a ceiling effect and the need for careful baseline calibration in preregistered LLM-for-NetOps trials. We report preregistration, execution manifest, raw outputs, verifier verdicts, and analysis artifacts and bound claims to the synthetic corpus, single model, and verifier used.

sections.introduction: Natural-language intent interfaces promise more accessible network operations, but operational adoption requires reliable translation of high-level intent into safe, correct low-level configuration sequences. Prior work shows LLMs can generate useful configuration templates yet frequently produce syntactic or semantic errors requiring downstream correction [1] and that verifier-guided generate→verify→repair pipelines can reduce errors for infrastructure artifacts [2], [3]. Agentic tool-using pipelines also expose claim-to-action vulnerabilities that motivate deterministic validation and gating [4]. We ask: Does combining constrained prompting (structured templates + explicit semantic slots) with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase semantic correctness for intent→configuration translation compared to an unconstrained baseline? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory trial design tailored to verifier-level outcomes; (2) a fully archived execution (N=150, paired episodes = 300) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network validator; (3) empirical evidence that, on a deterministically generated synthetic corpus matched to verifier capacity, constrained+verifier single-repair yields negligible absolute improvement relative to an already high-performing baseline; and (4) a failure-mode and methodological diagnosis emphasizing ceiling effects and preregistration calibration.
sections.related_work: Three literature strands guided our study. First, intent-to-configuration and NL→formal-spec translation work documents modest semantic-correctness in many benchmarked settings and the challenge of producing verifier-sound specifications from free text [1]. Second, verifier-aware generation and iterative repair (generate→verify→repair) have improved correctness in IaC and configuration tasks when paired with deterministic or policy-guided verifiers [2], [6]. Third, security analyses demonstrate that agentic pipelines that convert textual claims into tool actions are vulnerable to prompt-injection and claim-to-action exploits, motivating verifier gating and auditable controls [4], [5]. Mature network-verification tools (e.g., NetKAT/KATch and related systems) provide deterministic oracles that can assess reachability, isolation, and policy constraints and thus serve as the endpoint for verifier-level correctness measurements [3], [6]. Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these strands by preregistering a paired trial that measures verifier pass/fail as the primary outcome.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 and frozen prior to observing outcomes (preregistration SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399). Design: paired binary comparison between (A) baseline free-text prompt and (C) constrained template prompt plus deterministic verifier-guided single-repair attempt (guarded). Execution contract used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent the same single initial model generation served as the starting candidate for both baseline and guarded conditions; only the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call based on deterministic verifier feedback. This shared_initial_candidate behavior implies that baseline success counts report the verifier pass/fail of the initial single-shot candidate, whereas guarded success counts report the verifier pass/fail after the guarded pipeline completed (post-repair if a repair was applied). Planned confirmatory sample: N=150 distinct synthetic intents (target: 50 per intent family), paired episodes = 300. Model and verifier: declared model = gpt-5-mini; verifier = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Runtime budget: at most one initial model call per task and at most one repair call per task; actual model calls used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1. Task corpus and topologies: deterministic synthetic intent generator restricted to four intent families and verifier-capable topologies (4–32 nodes). Inclusion/exclusion: pre-call rule-based ambiguity detector and parser/coverage exclusions applied deterministically; none were excluded during the run. Primary estimand and analysis: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline assessed via exact McNemar two-sided test; 95% CIs via paired bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Multiplicity: two secondary contrasts were specified with Bonferroni correction. Missingness and retry: deterministic one-retry policy for transient API failures; analysis uses complete-pair primary treatment (complete_pair_count = 150). All mapping code, verifier inputs, raw outputs, and logs were archived in the execution bundle.
sections.results: Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 300 (complete_pair_count = 150), model_calls_used = 151, repair-stage_count = 1. Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0066666667 (0.67 percentage points). Statistical test: exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the difference = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair diagnostics: only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). Missingness/exclusions/contamination: none observed. Interpretation of shared_initial_candidate semantics (explicit): the baseline rate above reports verifier verdicts on the single initial model generation for each task; the guarded rate reports the final verifier verdict after the guarded pipeline completed (post-repair where invoked). Because the initial candidates were overwhelmingly valid (149/150), the guarded pipeline had only one opportunity to alter a failing initial candidate and did so once, producing the single additional guarded success. The preregistered power calculus assumed a much lower baseline (~35%) and targeted a 15 percentage-point absolute increase; the observed near-ceiling baseline invalidated that calibration and produced a null/practically negligible confirmatory result.
sections.discussion: Summary interpretation: constrained prompting plus a deterministic verifier-guided single-repair produced no material improvement over an already high-performing baseline on the preregistered synthetic corpus. This outcome reflects a ceiling effect rather than evidence that verifier guidance is universally unnecessary. Operational implications: (1) when base-model correctness is near 100% on representative tasks, single-repair guarded pipelines yield marginal returns; (2) guarded pipelines retain operational value for auditability, explicit validation, and defensive gating even when pass rates do not change; (3) preregistered confirmatory trials must calibrate baseline competence via pilot studies to avoid mismatched power assumptions. Relation to prior work: our result aligns with reports that verifier-guided methods can yield meaningful gains on harder or more diverse benchmarks [2], [3], but that gains shrink when tasks are simpler or models are highly capable on the chosen corpus. Methodological lesson: shared_initial_candidate semantics produce paired contrasts that isolate the marginal effect of the guarded repair step given a common initial candidate; authors designing future paired trials should choose generation semantics (shared vs independent initial samples) consistent with their scientific estimand. Limitations and future directions: see Limitations section; notably, independent initial-sample semantics or larger repair budgets might yield different outcomes and are natural directions for follow-up confirmatory work.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial measuring verifier-level semantic correctness for intent→configuration translation using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network validator. On the deterministically generated synthetic corpus the constrained prompting plus verifier-guided single-repair workflow increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (0.67 percentage points), a numerically small and statistically non-significant change under the preregistered test (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific outcome is methodological: preregistered LLM-for-NetOps trials must carefully calibrate baseline competence to avoid ceiling effects that mask potential benefits of verifier-guided repair. Technically, our result does not refute prior findings that verifier guidance helps in harder or more heterogeneous settings; it bounds the benefit on the specific synthetic corpus, single model, and verifier used in this run.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to a single guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned effect size 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures verifier pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim full operational safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
